sections.text: A pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic drug-drug interaction study of dorzagliatin and empagliflozin in patients with type 2 diabetes and obesity: an open-label phase I trial

Combination therapy of glucokinase activators and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors may exhibit potent glucose-lowering effects and improvement of β-cell function and insulin sensitivity in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus, given their complementary mechanisms of action. However, the safety, pharmacokinetic interactions and pharmacodynamic effects of such combinations remain unexplored. To address this gap, we conduct an open-label, sequential phase I trial (ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT03790787) evaluating the dorzagliatin and the sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor empagliflozin in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity in the US. After strict screening against the inclusion/exclusion criteria, 16 participants are deemed eligible. Participants receive sequential treatments—empagliflozin alone, empagliflozin plus dorzagliatin, and dorzagliatin alone—five days for each regimen, followed by a comprehensive assessment of pharmacokinetic profiles and safety. The primary outcomes included GMR for Cmax and AUC0-24h of empagliflozin and dorzagliatin of pharmacokinetic parameters and the incidence of adverse events, abnormal vital signs, abnormal clinical laboratory findings, and 12-lead electrocardiogram abnormalities of safety profile. A total of 27 adverse events occurs in 9 participants (56.3%), the majority of which are mild, with the exception of one case of moderate constipation. No clinically significant findings or changes attributable to study drug treatment were found in clinical chemistry, hematology and urinary analyses, and observed in vital signs, 12-lead electrocardiogram and physical examination. The geomean ratio and their associated 90% confidence intervals for both maximum plasma concentration (empagliflozin: 98.43% (84.07%, 115.25%); dorzagliatin: 103.94% (90.45%, 119.44%)) and area under the concentration-time curve from 0 to 24 h (empagliflozin: 97.53% (94.35%, 100.82%); dorzagliatin: 99.65% (95.25%, 104.25%)) of empagliflozin and dorzagliatin fall entirely within the conventional bioequivalence range of 80.00% to 125.00%. No pharmacokinetic drug-drug interaction is observed, and the treatment exhibits a favorable safety profile with good overall tolerability.

Dorzagliatin and empagliflozin combination therapy may improve β-cell function and insulin sensitivity in patients with type 2 diabetes and obesity. Here, the authors show that combination therapy exhibits a favorable safety profile with no PK interaction.
Introduction

Global diabetes prevalence is projected to rise dramatically, with modeling studies estimating more than 1.31 billion cases by 2050, approximately 96% of which will be type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Despite the availability of ten distinct classes of glucose-lowering drugs, only 60% of diagnosed patients achieve glycemic targets, reflecting the urgent requirement for mechanistically complementary combination strategies. Current American Diabetes Association (ADA) guidelines advocate combination therapy targeting multiple pathological pathways when monotherapy fails to achieve glycemic control in T2DM. By extending beyond its role in improving glycemic control over monotherapy, this strategy more effectively attenuates the natural progression of T2DM. Glucokinase activators (GKAs) represent a novel class of glucose-lowering drugs with a unique dual mechanism: they enhance glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS) via pancreatic β-cell sensitization while simultaneously promoting the release of endogenous glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1). Dorzagliatin, the first-in-class glucokinase activator (GKA) approved and currently marketed in China as HuaTangNing®, has demonstrated significant improvements in β-cell function (BCF) and induced diabetes remission in 52% of Chinese patients with T2DM during prospective follow-up. Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2is) exert the glucose-lowering effects primarily via selective inhibition of glucose reabsorption in the renal proximal tubules and are preferentially recommended for T2DM patients with concomitant cardiovascular or renal disease. Given their complementary mechanisms of action, the GKA and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor (SGLT2i) combination was anticipated to provide synergistic benefits: enhanced glycemic control, improved BCF and insulin sensitivity (IS), reduced complication risk, and increased long-term T2DM remission rates, which was urgent to be uncovered. Moreover, the pharmacokinetics (PK) interactions and pharmacodynamics (PD), along with the safety profile of this specific drug combination, have not been systematically elucidated. Increase of insulin resistance (IR) and decline in BCF are the core pathological changes underlying the progression of diabetes. Among existing assessment methods, the oral minimal model (OMM) stands as the unique model-based approach capable of accurately quantitatively evaluating phase-specific BCF and overall IS with high efficiency. It has been widely applied in both drug development and clinical practice based on a mixed-meal or an oral glucose tolerance test (MTT/OGTT) as practical alternatives to the hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp. However, this method just estimates these parameters individually, it requires complex clinical procedure with rich data (9 blood sampling time points per person) and leads to time-consuming clinical procedures and computational estimation. In order to systematically address the potential activity of dorzagliatin-empagliflozin combination effect on glucose-lowering and BCF/IS, we will firstly conduct a clinical trial evaluating the combination therapy of dorzagliatin and empagliflozin in patients with T2DM to characterize the PK, PD, and safety profile of dorzagliatin-empagliflozin combination therapy in T2DM patients, then we will mechanistically evaluate BCF and IS using newly developed population OMM method with NONMEM package. The combination therapy demonstrated superior glycemic control compared with either monotherapy, particularly against empagliflozin, as demonstrated by enhanced glucose-lowering efficacy, increased C-peptide secretion, and significant improvements in BCF and IS.

The clinical trial has been completed. The demographic characteristics of the study participants are presented in Table 1. The 16 enrolled participants were assigned to a sequence of three drug treatments. Fifteen participants (93.8%) completed the study and received all planned study medication doses, and one participant discontinued after morning dose of empagliflozin 25 mg on Day 5 due to adverse event of syncope. All outcomes, except for safety evaluations and demographic data, were derived from the 15 participants who completed the trial.

We systematically assessed the safety and tolerability profile by reviewing all individual participant data. A total of 27 adverse events (AEs) were reported in 9 participants (56.3%) during the study. The majority of AEs were assessed as mild in intensity, except for one participant with constipation that was moderate in intensity. There were 3 AEs reported in 3 participants (18.8%) during the empagliflozin run-in period including 2 AEs of mild constipation and 1 AE of mild genital pruritus. One AE of mild constipation in 1 participant was assessed as possibly related to empagliflozin and the other AE of mild constipation in 1 participant was assessed as unlikely related to empagliflozin. The AE of mild genital pruritus was assessed as unlikely related to empagliflozin. A total of 24 treatment-emergent AEs (TEAEs) were reported in 9 (56.3%) participants. The most common TEAEs involved metabolism and nutrition disorders (5 of 16 participants, 31.3%), gastrointestinal disorders (4 of 16 participants, 25.0%), eye disorders (2 of 16 participants, 12.5%), and nervous system disorders (2 of 16 participants, 12.5%). Individual TEAEs reported in more than 1 subject included hypoglycemic in 4 participants (25.0%), vision blurred in 2 participants (12.5%), and constipation in 2 participants (12.5%). One participant was early discontinued from the study due to the adverse event of mild syncope after the morning dose of empagliflozin alone on Day 5. Ten TEAEs, except hypoglycemia events, in 3 participants (18.75%) were considered possibly related to study drug treatment. They included AEs of constipation, vision blurred, chest pain and hyperkalemia in 1 participant possibly related to both dorzagliatin and empagliflozin, and constipation in 1 participant, dizziness in 2 participants, vomiting and syncope in 1 participant possibly related to empagliflozin treatment alone. Two participants reported hypoglycemia with blood glucose <54 mg/dL on Day 10 when receiving empagliflozin and dorzagliatin, and were assessed possibly related and related to empagliflozin and dorzagliatin treatment. All hypoglycemic events resolved without sequelae among participants who ingested apple juice or received no treatment. During this study, no deaths or serious AEs were reported, and no additional interventions were required throughout the trial period. Compared with either empagliflozin or dorzagliatin monotherapy, combination therapy was associated with a mild increase in the frequency and severity of AEs (Table 2). Overall, multiple doses of dorzagliatin alone (75 mg BID, twice a day) or in combination with empagliflozin (25 mg QD, once a day) were shown to be safe and well-tolerated.

For empagliflozin, the PK parameters (Cmax and AUC0-24 h) remained consistent whether administered as monotherapy or in combination with dorzagliatin. The geomean ratio (GMR) for empagliflozin (combination/monotherapy) were 98.43% (90% CI, 84.07%, 115.25%) for Cmax, and 97.53% (90% CI, 94.35%, 100.82%) for AUC0-24 h (Table 3). Similarly, dorzagliatin exposure, as reflected by Cmax and AUC0-24 h, was comparable between monotherapy and combination therapy with empagliflozin. The corresponding GMR for dorzagliatin were 103.94% (90% CI, 90.45%, 119.44%) for Cmax, and 99.65% (90% CI, 95.25%, 104.25%) for AUC0-24 h (Table 3).The GMR and their associated 90% confidence intervals (CI) for both Cmax and AUC0-24 h of empagliflozin and dorzagliatin fell entirely within the conventional bioequivalence range of 80.00% to 125.00%. These results indicate that coadministration of empagliflozin and dorzagliatin does not significantly alter the PK profile of either agent.
Secondary outcomes

The combination treatment demonstrated a significantly enhanced glucose-lowering effect compared with monotherapy with either empagliflozin (p < 0.0001, |Cohen’s d | =2.28) or dorzagliatin (p = 0.017, |Cohen’s d | =1.13) (Fig. 1a). The iAUC0-4 h of glucose during the OGTT was 465.10 ± 161.28 mg·h/dL with empagliflozin monotherapy, 290.30 ± 98.87 mg·h/dL with empagliflozin plus dorzagliatin combination therapy, and 381.00 ± 104.25 mg·h/dL with dorzagliatin monotherapy (Fig. 1a). The combination treatment showed a statistically significant increase in C-peptide secretion compared with empagliflozin (p = 0.030, |Cohen’s d | =1.10) under glucose-stimulated conditions. Although an upward trend was observed relative to dorzagliatin monotherapy, this difference did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.19, |Cohen’s d | =0.714) (Fig. 1b). The iAUC0-4 h of C-peptide during the OGTT was 11.47 ± 4.22 ng·h/mL with empagliflozin monotherapy, 14.95 ± 8.25 ng·h/mL with empagliflozin plus dorzagliatin combination therapy, and 12.42 ± 6.16 ng·h/mL with dorzagliatin monotherapy (Fig. 1b).

The combination therapy did not lead to a significant increase in insulin secretion compared with empagliflozin monotherapy. (p = 0.18, |Cohen’s d | =0.72). Compared with dorzagliatin monotherapy, the combination therapy showed no statistically significant difference in insulin secretion (p = 0.52), with a small-to-medium effect size (|Cohen’s d | =0.44), as depicted in Fig. 1c. The iAUC0-4 h of insulin during the OGTT was 96.05 ± 35.64 μIU·h/mL with empagliflozin monotherapy, 118.39 ± 62.90 μIU·h/mL with empagliflozin plus dorzagliatin combination therapy, and 103.43 ± 46.14 μIU·h/mL with dorzagliatin monotherapy (Fig. 1c).

As a widely adopted metric for assessing BCF, the insulin secretion-sensitivity index-2 (ISSI-2) was significantly elevated during combination therapy compared with either empagliflozin (p < 0.001, |Cohen’s d | =1.75) or dorzagliatin (p < 0.001, |Cohen’s d | =1.79) with values of 170.87 ± 78.13 for empagliflozin + dorzagliatin, 119.48 ± 44.97 for empagliflozin monotherapy, and 113.12 ± 42.09 for dorzagliatin monotherapy, respectively (Fig. 1d).

IS evaluation results of the population OMM
Model validation

OGTT data from three treatment groups were utilized to develop a population oral glucose minimal model sharing a common structural framework. Potential covariates were systematically screened. However, none of the initially considered variables met the predefined criteria for inclusion. Consequently, the final model was constructed without incorporating any covariates. The estimated parameter values are provided in Supplementary Appendix A, Table S1. Notably, the coefficients of variation (CV) derived from the 15 individual patient datasets were relatively high, indicating substantial inter-individual variability. Model evaluation results were presented in Supplementary Appendix A, including: (1) goodness-of-fit (GOF) plots (Fig. S1); (2) bootstrap validation results (Table S1); (3) visual predictive checks (VPC, Fig. S3); (4) individual fittings (Fig. S5). The model was deemed acceptable based on standard modeling evaluation criteria.

Based on individually estimated IS index derived from the model, statistical results were summarized in Fig. 2. The analysis demonstrated that combination therapy with empagliflozin and dorzagliatin significantly improved IS compared with empagliflozin monotherapy. Specifically, a mean difference of 2.52 was observed between the combination treatment and empagliflozin alone (empagliflozin + dorzagliatin (6.37 ± 2.41) vs. empagliflozin (3.85 ± 1.85), p < 0.0001, |Cohen’s d | =1.87). However, the comparison between the combination of empagliflozin and dorzagliatin and dorzagliatin monotherapy did not achieve sufficient statistical power to detect a significant difference (empagliflozin + dorzagliatin (6.37 ± 2.41) vs. dorzagliatin (5.75 ± 0.92), p = 0.42, |Cohen’s d | =0.17).

Discussion

Dorzagliatin and empagliflozin exert their glucose-lowering effects through distinct yet complementary mechanisms and demonstrated favorable compatibility in the present study, as evidenced by the absence of PK interactions and an excellent tolerability profile. These results provide a robust pharmacological foundation for developing a fixed-dose combination therapy, which may enable synergistic improvements in glycemic control, BCF, and IS without necessitating dose adjustments.

In T2DM patients, impaired first-phase insulin secretion represents a well-characterized pathophysiological abnormality. This defect contributes directly to postprandial hyperglycemia and is associated with an increased risk of long-term diabetic complications. As a GKA, dorzagliatin enhances the enzyme’s sensitivity to glucose fluctuations, effectively restoring the physiological glucose threshold for insulin release. Given that the rate of intracellular glucose metabolism is a key determinant of GSIS, dorzagliatin potentiates this fundamental pathway and facilitates the recovery of early-phase insulin response. In contrast, empagliflozin lacks direct regulatory effects on pancreatic β-cells and does not modulate the signaling pathways responsible for first-phase insulin secretion. Therefore, within the combination therapy, the observed enhancement in the dynamic insulin secretory phase—as indicated by improved dynamic BCF index (φd)—can be primarily attributed to the glucose-sensitizing action of dorzagliatin, which specifically restores glucose-stimulated first-phase insulin release (Fig. 3b).

The combination therapy produced a significantly greater improvement in static-phase BCF (φs) compared with either empagliflozin or dorzagliatin monotherapy (Fig. 3c). In the postprandial state, elevated circulating glucose levels persist for several hours and account for 60–70% of total insulin secretion. The regulation of this sustained, amplifying phase of GSIS involves synergistic interactions among multiple signaling pathways. Empagliflozin contributes to this process by promoting urinary glucose excretion, which mitigates glucotoxicity and lipotoxicity, thereby helping to preserve functional β-cell mass—a mechanism that has gained broad recognition. Dorzagliatin, on the other hand, has been demonstrated to stimulate GLP-1 secretion. Previous studies indicate that dorzagliatin monotherapy elicits higher circulating levels of total GLP-1 compared with sitagliptin monotherapy. Notably, the same study revealed that the combination of dorzagliatin and sitagliptin increased active GLP-1 levels by 38% relative to sitagliptin monotherapy. Dorzagliatin exerts its glucose-lowering effects by sensing elevated blood glucose levels. Consequently, its direct action in promoting GLP-1-regulated pathways occurs primarily in the postprandial state. These effects are believed to be potential mechanisms for the enhancement of the amplifying phase of GSIS ability. In this study, the marked improvement in the static-phase BCF (φs) following combination therapy, as compared to monotherapy, indicates a considerable synergistic effect of both drugs on enhancing sustained insulin secretion.

Given that the amplifying phase accounts for a substantially greater proportion of total insulin release than the trigger phase, the overall pancreatic function index closely mirrors the pattern of amplifying-phase secretion capacity. Consequently, a significant difference was observed between the combination therapy and either monotherapy (Fig. 3d). The index φtot was corroborated by the ISSI-2, as calculated using a previously simplified formula.

The combination therapy produced a statistically significant improvement in basal BCF (φb) compared with empagliflozin monotherapy (Fig. 3a). While empagliflozin contributes to the improvement of BCF under reduced blood glucose conditions, it concurrently stimulates fasting glucagon secretion from pancreatic α-cells. Additionally, glucokinase as a glucose sensor, primarily regulates the level of insulin release in response to glucose stimulation, with little response in fasting insulin secretion especially in short-term drug administration. Based on their distinct mechanisms of action as monotherapies, improving basal islet function is not a direct pharmacological effect of either drug. Consequently, the enhancement of basal BCF likely depends on the comprehensive restoration of systemic islet homeostasis. In this study, the marked increase in φb observed in the combination therapy group indicates that short-term co-administration can significantly enhance basal BCF. This improvement suggests that the combination therapy may provide superior control of fasting blood glucose in clinical practice. However, the precise molecular mechanisms underlying this synergistic effect warrant further investigation.

Dorzagliatin has demonstrated potential in restoring impaired BCF in patients with T2DM; however, its direct effect on IR remains limited based on its mechanism of action, although reductions in homeostatic model assessment for insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) have been observed in clinical trials. Empagliflozin contributes to the amelioration of insulin resistance by alleviating glucotoxicity and lipotoxicity, as well as by enhancing IS in peripheral tissues—particularly the liver and skeletal muscle.In the present study, dorzagliatin significantly improved IS compared with empagliflozin monotherapy (p < 0.001). This effect may be attributed to the complementary action of dorzagliatin on glucagon regulation: Dorzagliatin has been shown to reduce glucagon secretion, thereby counterbalancing the empagliflozin-induced rise in glucagon that accompanies urinary glucose excretion. The combination therapy may further ameliorate glucotoxicity, thereby enhancing IS. The DI serves as an integrated measure of glucose disposal capacity with combination assessments of pancreatic BCF and peripheral IS. It is calculated as the product of BCF (in a given secretory phase) and IS. Since IS remains constant across secretory phases, changes in DI primarily reflect alterations in BCF. Consistent with this physiological principle, the results of this study demonstrate that changes in DI following combination therapy align closely with phase-specific improvements in BCF. The combination therapy demonstrated a significant improvement in glycemic disposal capacity compared with either empagliflozin or dorzagliatin monotherapy.

Dorzagliatin monotherapy has achieved a diabetes remission rate of 52%, with analyses demonstrating strong positive correlations (r > 0.80) between remission duration and key functional indices, including BCF, IS, and DI. These results support the promising strategy of developing optimized dorzagliatin-based combination therapies to further improve rates of diabetes remission. In the present short-term combination study, significant improvements in IS, and different phase BCF, different phase DI were observed compared with monotherapy, indicating the potential for enhanced long-term disease management. Further long-term trials are warranted to determine whether the combination can further increase the remission rate and to elucidate which specific phase of BCF recovery most strongly predicts sustained remission.

In comparison with the individual OMM method, the population OMM approach demonstrated strong correlation (r > 0.8) across most parameter estimates, with the exception of φd (r = 0.64). Furthermore, the population OMM significantly reduced computational time by at least 10-fold and achieved a higher rate of successful model convergence. Although its application is supported by well-established physiological principles, OMM method lacks formal validation under conditions of SGLT2i-induced glycosuria. We acknowledge this as a study limitation and propose future studies incorporating targeted analyses in populations with pronounced SGLT2i-induced glycosuria would be valuable to further confirm the robustness of the model predictions under these conditions.

Since the primary objectives of this clinical trial were to investigate the PK drug-drug interactions (DDI) and safety, with the secondary objective being the evaluation of the PD interaction, the sample size calculation and dosing duration were determined based on the respective PK profiles of dorzagliatin and empagliflozin. The relatively small sample size and short treatment duration may raise concerns regarding the reliability of the PD outcomes. However, effect size analysis indicated that only the comparisons for insulin iAUC0–4 h, IS, and φb showed relatively low credibility (|Cohen’s d | <0.7), while the results for other parameters were highly reliable. Therefore, these limitations do not affect the overall conclusions of this study. Compared with the long-term medication requirements in the clinical management of diabetes, the present study is limited by its relatively short duration for evaluating therapeutic efficacy. Long-term treatment outcomes in individual patients are influenced by multiple factors, including disease progression, environmental variables, and lifestyle habits. While this study provides foundational evidence regarding the efficacy of the combination therapy, the long-term benefits of this regimen remain to be further investigated in extended clinical trials.

In summary, this clinical study demonstrated that the combination of empagliflozin and dorzagliatin was well-tolerated and exhibited no PK interactions in patients with T2DM and obesity. The combination therapy elicited a more potent glucose-lowering effect compared with either monotherapy. Analyses based on the population model indicated that the combined regimen improved IS, along with basal-, dynamic-, static-phase and overall BCF, as well as the DI, across various magnitudes. These short-term improvements in BCF and IS provide a rationale for evaluating long-term combination strategies. Building upon the observed improvements in BCF and IS, the combination of a GKA and an SGLT2i demonstrates strong potential for enhancing the management of T2DM. This multifunctional therapeutic strategy offers a distinct and promising advantage over monotherapy approaches.
Methods
Clinical trial administration

This is a phase 1, non-randomized, open-label (unblinded), sequential clinical study. This study was designed to evaluate the safety and PK, PD profiles of dorzagliatin and empagliflozin as monotherapies and in combination in patients with T2DM and obesity. It was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03790787). Additionally, PD parameters were mainly evaluated by population OMM. This study protocol was reviewed and approved prior to initiation by Integ Review Ethics Review Board (Austin, USA), an independent, FDA-registered central Institutional Review Board (IRB). Integ Review IRB provides ethical approval covering all participating study sites, including those located in New Jersey. In accordance with U.S. regulations (21 CFR Parts 50 and 56), approval by a duly constituted central IRB is sufficient and does not require separate local IRB approvals at each study center unless mandated by institutional policy. All study activities at the clinical sites in New Jersey were conducted under the approved protocol and in compliance with applicable federal and state regulations. All registered outcome measures -both primary and secondary-were systematically aligned with the master protocol to ensure full terminological and methodological consistency in endpoint definitions, evaluation criteria, and analysis timelines. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants before study commencement. The study was conducted in compliance with the Declaration of Helsinki, the International Conference on Harmonization Good Clinical Practice (ICH-GCP) guidelines, and US Food and Drug Administration regulations. The Research complies with all relevant ethical regulations.
Sample size

At least 15 evaluable participants in the sequence will be required to achieve a power of at least 0.8 for the GMR between two treatments (empagliflozin + dorzagliatin vs. dorzagliatin alone or empagliflozin + dorzagliatin vs. empagliflozin alone) for Cmax or AUC0-24h, with the equivalence bounds of 0.8 to 1.25, assuming a true GMR of 1 and an intra-subject variability (CV) of 20.2%, in an equivalence test using two one-sided tests at a significance level of 0.05. The intra-subject variability for empagliflozin Cmax and AUC0-24h is reported to be 20.2% and 7.8%, respectively. The intra-subject variability for dorzagliatin Cmax and AUC0-24h is estimated to be 14.0% and 6.2%, respectively. Therefore, to ensure a satisfactory DDI assessment, and assuming a drop-out rate of 15%, we plan to enroll 18 eligible participants by aiming to obtain 15 evaluable participants for DDI assessment.

Study design

This phase I, non-randomized, open-label (unblinded), single-sequence, multiple-dose trial was conducted at two clinical sites (Frontage Clinical Services, Inc., Secaucus, NJ, and BIOTRIAL INC., Newark, NJ). Prior to enrollment, all participants were required to switch their existing glucose-lowering regimen to empagliflozin 25 mg once daily for a minimum of 14 days. Throughout the 12-day run-in period, AEs were recorded for all participants. Eligible individuals were subsequently admitted to the clinical research center on Day -2 and remained hospitalized for 18 consecutive nights until discharge on Day 17, following the completion of all study procedures. The gender of the participants was assigned without considering the influence factor of gender. The low sample size (10 females and 6 males) in this study did not allow for meaningful conclusions to be drawn, and that the study was not suitable for gender categorization. A total of 16 participants were enrolled, with a mean age of 55.56 ± 9.27 years. The first participant was enrolled on March 21, 2019, and the last participant was enrolled on February 6, 2020. All eligible participants were sequentially assigned to three treatment regimens: empagliflozin 25 mg QD for 5 days (Days 1–5), followed by empagliflozin 25 mg QD plus dorzagliatin 75 mg BID for 5 days (Days 6–10), and subsequently dorzagliatin 75 mg BID alone for 5 days (Days 11–15). On Days 5, 10, and 15, blood samples for PK analysis were collected over a 24-h period following the morning dose. All medications were administered 60 min prior to meals. On the PK sampling days (Days 5, 10, and 15), an OGTT was performed, during which participants ingested a 75-g glucose solution 30 ( ± 5) min after study drug administration instead of a standard breakfast. Throughout the entire treatment period, the use of illicit drugs, alcohol, tobacco-containing products, and food or beverages containing caffeine was prohibited. Additionally, the administration of any drugs known to affect CYP3A4 activity, herbal products, prescription medications (other than the study drugs), or OTC products was not permitted.
Study outcomes

The study outcomes were pre-defined as follows. The primary pharmacokinetic outcomes included GMR for Cmax and AUC0-24h of empagliflozin and dorzagliatin, which were central to the hypothesis testing and formed the basis for the sample size calculation. The primary safety outcomes included the incidence of adverse events, abnormal vital signs, abnormal clinical laboratory findings, and 12-lead electrocardiogram abnormalities. The secondary outcomes comprising iAUC0-4h of glucose, insulin and C-peptide, were assessed to evaluate the PD responses. Detailed analyses of the other secondary endpoints, such as plasma glucagon and urinary glucose excretion, will be presented in a subsequent dedicated manuscript, ensuring comprehensive and rigorous evaluation. Furthermore, exploratory analyses of ISSI-II, IS, φb, φd, φs, φtot, dynamic-phase DI, static-phase DI, and total DI were conducted to provide supportive evidence on additional aspects of PD evaluation.
Sample collection of PK and PD

On Days 5, 10 and 15, blood samples for plasma PK analysis were collected at the following time points: pre-dose, and 0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 18, 24 h after dosing using an indwelling catheter or direct venipuncture. A total of 42 blood samples (approximately 6 mL each) were collected from each subject into K2EDTA tubes for determination of dorzagliatin and empagliflozin concentration and PK assessments. Contents of tube were mixed thoroughly with gentle inversion at least 8 times to mix the anti-coagulant and stored on wet ice for no more than 30 min before centrifugation at approximately 4 °C ~2000 × g for 10 min. The harvested plasma was split into two approximately equal aliquots and stored in appropriate size cryovial tubes. Plasma samples were stored at −70 ( ± 10) °C within approximately 60 min of harvesting pending shipment to the bioanalytical laboratory for analysis. On these same days, an OGTT was performed, where participants ingested a 75 g glucose solution after administration of the study drug. For the OGTT, blood samples were obtained immediately before glucose intake (pre-dose), and at 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, and 4 h thereafter to measure serum concentrations of glucose, C-peptide, and insulin. A total of 24 blood samples of approximately 5 mL each for measurement of serum glucose, insulin, and C-peptide. Ultimately, a total of 412 samples were analyzed and reported for dorzagliatin and empagliflozin concentrations in human plasma. 360, 356, and 355 samples were analyzed and reported for glucose, insulin, and C-peptide concentrations in human serum, respectively.

Safety assessments were performed consistently during the study, including clinical laboratory analyses, vital sign (blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate and oral temperature) measurements, physical examinations, 12-lead electrocardiograms and AEs. Population oral C-peptide minimal model

The population oral C-peptide minimal model is adapted from the reference minimal model. This model leverages time-course glucose and C-peptide concentration data obtained from OGTT to characterize C-peptide kinetics (secretion distribution, and elimination). Glucose-dependent regulation of C-peptide secretion mediated by the rate of glucose change which represent dynamic stimulation and the absolute glucose concentration which reflect sustained stimulation. The model is formalized through a system of differential equations that capture: C-peptide secretion driven by the rate of glucose change; C-peptide secretion proportional to the absolute glucose elevation; distribution of C-peptide in the central compartment and distribution of C-peptide in the peripheral compartment. Kd_GSIS is the coefficient quantifying the strength of secretion function induced by rapid glucose changes. β is a parameter representing the amplitude of the secretion function triggered by absolute glucose elevation. Statistical analysis

A mixed model for the sequential design was used for analyzing the PK parameters Cmax and AUC0-24h based on natural log-transformed values, with treatment as fixed effect and participants as random effect. A point estimate and the corresponding 90% CI for the difference between least squares means of the two treatments was calculated. The point estimate and the corresponding 90% CI was then back-transformed (natural exponentiated) to obtain a point estimate and the 90% CI for the GMR in the original scale. All PD parameters were calculated from repeatedly measured clinical outcomes. A mixed-effects modeling approach was therefore preferred for analysis, as it accounts for and separates mixed-effects variations, thereby yielding estimates of the fixed effects. The analytical procedure began with testing the normality of all parameters; non-normally distributed data were log-transformed and reassessed for normality. For data that were normally distributed either in raw or log-transformed form, a linear mixed-effects model was applied, followed by validation of residual homogeneity of variance. Data that remained non-normal after transformation or failed the homogeneity test were analyzed using a generalized linear mixed-effects model. For all parameters, post-hoc analyses were performed to obtain p-values for between-group comparisons, and effect sizes (|Cohen’s d | ) were calculated. The inflation of type I error rate attributable to multiple comparisons was mitigated by applying appropriate statistical corrections: the Holm method for p-values derived from mixed-effects models and the Dunnett method for all post-hoc pairwise comparisons.PK parameters (Cmax and AUC0-24h) were analyzed using SAS (version 9.4), while iAUC0-4 h of glucose, insulin and C-peptide, ISSI-2, φ, IS, and DI were evaluated using R (version 4.5.1). The R code used for the statistical analyses is available in Supplementary Appendix C.

Parameters derived from the OMM and the population OMM were compared via linear regression analysis performed in GraphPad Prism (version 9.0) to determine the correlation coefficient (r) and the associated p-value for significance.
